When you report bad news to a committee, your first minute decides everything. Here are three rules. First, lead with the number. Do not downplay it, and do not hide it on the last slide. Say it clearly: we are two hundred thousand dollars over budget. Second, explain the root cause in one sentence, and do not blame another team. Even though the problem may not be yours, you are accountable for the solution. Third, balance the bad news with a plan. This is where small words like although and despite help you. For example: although we are over budget, the go-live date has not changed. Or: despite the setback, the risk is under control. One sentence like that tells the committee two things: you are honest, and you are in control. Remember, committees forgive problems. They do not forgive surprises.

Good morning, everyone. I will start with the difficult part. The payroll bridge is two hundred thousand dollars over budget, which is about eight percent. The root cause was testing. We found errors in the old payroll data, and we needed three extra weeks of tests to fix them. Although this was not in the original plan, I believe it was the right decision, because the alternative was paying people the wrong salaries. Here is how we will mitigate the impact. We will use one hundred and twenty thousand dollars from the contingency budget, and savings in the travel budget will offset another fifty thousand. Despite the extra cost, the go-live date of March first has not changed. Carlos and I are happy to take your questions.
